sources.title: Inventaire linguistique des contenus clés aux niveaux du CECR (Eaquals & CIEP, 2015)
sources.scope: Read the full PDF (112 pages; printed page = PDF page − 2), downloaded from the Eaquals resource page. Itemised: Annexe E A1 and A2 key-content lists (pp. 56–58, every entry, read from rendered page images to fix column order); Annexe D référentiel (pp. 44–54): rows whose A1 or A2 cell is lightly shaded (« moins clé ») and that are not already key at or below that level, read visually because shading is not machine-readable; Annexe C text types (pp. 40–43), every row with a shaded A1 or A2 cell; Annexe B A1 and A2 scenarios (pp. 22–29), competences and strategies; Annexe F A1/A2 language realisations (pp. 62–73), headings checked and four points absent from Annexes D/E registered. Sections 2, 4 and 5 (purpose, structure, non-exhaustiveness) read. L'Inventaire (§5, p. 14–15) présente des contenus clés « non exhaustifs » et ne détaille ni l'orthographe ni la prononciation (seul le scénario A2 « Partir en vacances » cite « liaisons, rythme, intonation »).
sources.licenseNote: Only item names, levels and page locators are registered. All English explanations, French examples and mastery criteria are original; no examples are copied from Annexe F.

sources.title: Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (Council of Europe, 2001)
sources.scope: Not re-read in this round. Cited only as the general frame for supplement units (pronunciation, orthography, writing, mediation, classroom language, varieties) that the Inventaire does not itemise; section numbers are given from the framework's structure and are unverified.

sourceUnits.label: Alphabet and letter names
sourceUnits.locator: CEFR 2001 §5.2.1.5 Orthographic competence
sourceUnits.rationale: L'Inventaire (§5, p. 14–15) présente des contenus clés « non exhaustifs » et ne détaille ni l'orthographe ni la prononciation (seul le scénario A2 « Partir en vacances » cite « liaisons, rythme, intonation »). Learners must spell names and addresses aloud (the Inventaire lists "épeler" at A1) before any of that is possible.

sourceUnits.label: Accents and diacritics (é è ê à ç ë ï)
sourceUnits.locator: CEFR 2001 §5.2.1.5 Orthographic competence
sourceUnits.rationale: L'Inventaire (§5, p. 14–15) présente des contenus clés « non exhaustifs » et ne détaille ni l'orthographe ni la prononciation (seul le scénario A2 « Partir en vacances » cite « liaisons, rythme, intonation »). Accents change pronunciation and sometimes meaning (a/à, ou/où) and must be read and written from the start.

sourceUnits.label: Sound–spelling correspondences (graphemes such as ou, oi, eau, an, on, in, ch, gn, qu)
sourceUnits.locator: CEFR 2001 §5.2.1.5 Orthographic competence / §5.2.1.6 Orthoepic competence
sourceUnits.rationale: L'Inventaire (§5, p. 14–15) présente des contenus clés « non exhaustifs » et ne détaille ni l'orthographe ni la prononciation (seul le scénario A2 « Partir en vacances » cite « liaisons, rythme, intonation »). French spelling maps several letters to one sound; without these rules learners cannot read new words aloud or spell words they hear.

sourceUnits.label: Silent letters and silent grammatical endings (-e, -s, -t, -ent)
sourceUnits.locator: CEFR 2001 §5.2.1.5 Orthographic competence
sourceUnits.rationale: L'Inventaire (§5, p. 14–15) présente des contenus clés « non exhaustifs » et ne détaille ni l'orthographe ni la prononciation (seul le scénario A2 « Partir en vacances » cite « liaisons, rythme, intonation »). Much of French grammar (plural, verb person, feminine) is written but not heard; reading and writing need an explicit rule set.

sourceUnits.label: Punctuation and typographic conventions (spaces before ? ! : ;, guillemets, capitals)
sourceUnits.locator: CEFR 2001 §5.2.1.5 Orthographic competence
sourceUnits.rationale: L'Inventaire (§5, p. 14–15) présente des contenus clés « non exhaustifs » et ne détaille ni l'orthographe ni la prononciation (seul le scénario A2 « Partir en vacances » cite « liaisons, rythme, intonation »). French typography differs from English (no capitals on days, months, nationality adjectives; spacing before high punctuation in France).

sourceUnits.label: Oral vowel contrasts (u/ou, é/è, e/é)
sourceUnits.locator: CEFR 2001 §5.2.1.4 Phonological competence
sourceUnits.rationale: L'Inventaire (§5, p. 14–15) présente des contenus clés « non exhaustifs » et ne détaille ni l'orthographe ni la prononciation (seul le scénario A2 « Partir en vacances » cite « liaisons, rythme, intonation »). Contrasts such as tu/tout and le/les carry meaning and are absent from English.

sourceUnits.label: Nasal vowels
sourceUnits.locator: CEFR 2001 §5.2.1.4 Phonological competence
sourceUnits.rationale: L'Inventaire (§5, p. 14–15) présente des contenus clés « non exhaustifs » et ne détaille ni l'orthographe ni la prononciation (seul le scénario A2 « Partir en vacances » cite « liaisons, rythme, intonation »). Nasal vowels distinguish words (beau/bon, vin/vent) and do not exist as phonemes in English.

sourceUnits.label: Consonants: French r, unaspirated p t k, final consonants
sourceUnits.locator: CEFR 2001 §5.2.1.4 Phonological competence
sourceUnits.rationale: L'Inventaire (§5, p. 14–15) présente des contenus clés « non exhaustifs » et ne détaille ni l'orthographe ni la prononciation (seul le scénario A2 « Partir en vacances » cite « liaisons, rythme, intonation »). The uvular r and the treatment of final consonants are the most audible features of an English-speaking accent.

sourceUnits.label: Elision, liaison and enchaînement
sourceUnits.locator: CEFR 2001 §5.2.1.4 Phonological competence
sourceUnits.rationale: L'Inventaire (§5, p. 14–15) présente des contenus clés « non exhaustifs » et ne détaille ni l'orthographe ni la prononciation (seul le scénario A2 « Partir en vacances » cite « liaisons, rythme, intonation »). Elision is obligatory in writing from the first lesson (je → j', le → l'); liaison changes how word groups sound.

sourceUnits.label: Rhythm, final-syllable stress and intonation
sourceUnits.locator: CEFR 2001 §5.2.1.4 Phonological competence
sourceUnits.rationale: L'Inventaire (§5, p. 14–15) présente des contenus clés « non exhaustifs » et ne détaille ni l'orthographe ni la prononciation (seul le scénario A2 « Partir en vacances » cite « liaisons, rythme, intonation »). Questions by intonation alone are the most common A1 question form, so rising intonation must be taught.

sourceUnits.label: Verb conjugation patterns (-er verbs, core irregular verbs)
sourceUnits.locator: CEFR 2001 §5.2.1.2 Grammatical competence
sourceUnits.rationale: L'Inventaire cite « Le présent (verbes réguliers + usuels) » sans dresser la liste des verbes ni des modèles de conjugaison; un cours doit fixer quels verbes irréguliers entrent en A1.

sourceUnits.label: Cognates and false friends (English–French)
sourceUnits.locator: CEFR 2001 §5.2.1.1 Lexical competence
sourceUnits.rationale: The A1 scenario lists "Chercher des mots apparentés" as a strategy; English speakers also need to know which look-alikes mislead (librairie, actuellement, rester).

sourceUnits.label: Regional varieties of French (France, Belgium, Switzerland, Québec)
sourceUnits.locator: CEFR 2001 §5.2.2.5 Dialect and accent
sourceUnits.rationale: L'Inventaire a été rédigé avec des partenaires suisses et canadiens et cite des exemples canadiens (fin de semaine, dollars) sans traiter la variation; learners meet these forms at A1 (septante, déjeuner/dîner).

sourceUnits.label: Spoken versus written French (dropping ne, on for nous, ça)
sourceUnits.locator: CEFR 2001 §5.2.2.4 Register differences
sourceUnits.rationale: Learners hear "je sais pas" and "on y va" from the first conversations; the Inventaire gives these spoken forms in examples but does not name the register difference.

sourceUnits.label: Short spoken monologue (describing oneself, one's day, a plan)
sourceUnits.locator: CEFR 2001 §4.4.1.1 Oral production
sourceUnits.rationale: The A1 scenario names "Monologue suivi" as a text; A1–A2 courses need a separate, assessable sustained-speech task.

sourceUnits.label: Writing short functional texts (notes, messages, postcards, emails)
sourceUnits.locator: CEFR 2001 §4.4.1.2 Written production / §4.4.3.4 Written interaction
sourceUnits.rationale: L'annexe C ne couvre que la réception; writing tasks appear only scattered in the scenarios, so a course needs explicit writing activities.

sourceUnits.label: Simple mediation (passing on information across languages)
sourceUnits.locator: CEFR 2001 §4.4.4 Mediating activities
sourceUnits.rationale: Mediation is not covered by the Inventaire at A1–A2 (the authors note that CEFR mediation was not calibrated); travellers and families relay simple information.

sourceUnits.label: Classroom language and instructions for young learners
sourceUnits.locator: CEFR 2001 §4.1.1 Domains (educational)
sourceUnits.rationale: L'Inventaire vise les apprenants de 16 ans et plus (§2, p. 4); a children's track needs the language of classroom routines.

units.title: Hello, letters and getting by in class
units.goal: Greets, thanks, apologises, gets attention and asks for repetition with fixed chunks; spells their name; follows classroom instructions
units.rationale: Grammar-free entry: real exchanges are possible from day one with memorised chunks, and the alphabet and tu/vous choice underpin everything that follows

units.title: The sounds and spelling of French
units.goal: Hears and produces the oral and nasal vowels and key consonants, reads accents, links sounds to common spellings and knows which final letters are silent
units.rationale: French spelling is far from its pronunciation; an early, explicit sound–spelling pass prevents fossilised reading errors in every later unit

units.title: Who I am: être, avoir and introductions
units.goal: Introduces themselves and others (name, nationality, country) with être, avoir, subject and tonic pronouns and c'est
units.rationale: The two most frequent verbs and the pronoun system are needed for almost every sentence; introductions give them an immediate use

units.title: Numbers, personal details and family
units.goal: Gives and understands numbers, dates of birth, addresses and phone numbers; talks about their family; asks yes/no questions; fills in a form
units.rationale: Personal information is the first real transaction (forms, registration); the 70–99 system needs dedicated practice

units.title: Things around me: gender, articles, il y a, negation
units.goal: Names everyday objects with the right gender and article, says what there is and is not
units.rationale: Gender and the article system are the backbone of the noun phrase; il y a and ne … pas allow first descriptions

units.title: Describing people and things
units.goal: Describes appearance, character, clothes and objects with agreeing adjectives, possessives and demonstratives
units.rationale: Agreement and adjective position build on gender and articles; description is a core A1 function

units.title: Daily routine and time
units.goal: Tells the time, gives dates and describes a daily routine with present-tense regular, irregular and reflexive verbs
units.rationale: The present-tense paradigms are introduced through the routine, where they are used repeatedly and naturally

units.title: Asking questions; weather and news
units.goal: Asks for information with question words and quel, talks about the weather and asks after people
units.rationale: Information questions need the present tense; this unit turns learners from responders into askers

units.title: Likes, leisure and invitations
units.goal: Talks about likes and leisure, invites, accepts and refuses, and congratulates with modal verbs and basic connectors
units.rationale: Modals (pouvoir, vouloir, devoir) unlock invitations and refusals; connectors start linking sentences

units.title: Food and shopping
units.goal: Buys food and goods, asks prices and quantities, and orders in a café or restaurant politely
units.rationale: The partitive and quantities are needed for the most common travel transaction; je voudrais is taught as a polite chunk

units.title: Places, directions and transport
units.goal: Locates places, asks for and follows directions, uses transport and describes their town
units.rationale: Place prepositions and the imperative are needed together for directions

units.title: Plans and the near future
units.goal: Talks about plans and holidays with aller + infinitive, recent past with venir de, necessity and purpose
units.rationale: The near future is formed with a known verb (aller) and gives a first time reference beyond the present

units.title: What I did: the passé composé
units.goal: Says what they did yesterday or last weekend with the passé composé and time indicators; describes a past moment with c'était
units.rationale: The first past tense comes after the present paradigms and the participle forms it reuses

units.title: Home, work and appointments
units.goal: Describes their home and job, makes appointments, and uses on and ça as in everyday speech
units.rationale: Consolidates A1 grammar in two key life domains and introduces the very frequent on

units.title: Reading and writing everyday texts
units.goal: Reads personal messages, public notices and tourist information; understands announcements; writes short messages and gives a short prepared talk
units.rationale: Integrates A1 into the text types and activities listed by the Inventaire, with reading/listening strategies and writing conventions

units.title: Telling a story in the past
units.goal: Narrates a sequence of past events with être/avoir agreement and chronological connectors; talks about work experience
units.rationale: Extends the A1 passé composé to connected narration, the central A2 function

units.title: Description in the past: the imparfait
units.goal: Describes past situations and habits with the imparfait and combines it with the passé composé; tells a short biography
units.rationale: The imparfait is only meaningful against the passé composé, so it follows narration directly

units.title: Future, conditions and wishes
units.goal: Talks about future events with the futur simple, real conditions with si + present, and wishes and intentions
units.rationale: The futur simple builds on infinitives and the conditional chunks already known

units.title: Object pronouns, y and en
units.goal: Replaces objects and places with le/la/les, lui/leur, y and en in the present and passé composé
units.rationale: Pronoun placement is a major French difficulty; it needs the verb constructions from A1

units.title: Pronouns and relative clauses
units.goal: Uses possessive, demonstrative and indefinite pronouns and links clauses with qui, que and où
units.rationale: Relatives and pronouns let learners build longer descriptions and definitions

units.title: Comparing and evaluating
units.goal: Compares people, places and products; says what they liked and disliked; uses exclamations and tout
units.rationale: Comparison and evaluation are needed before opinions and choices

units.title: Opinions, agreement and reasons
units.goal: Agrees and disagrees, gives and asks for opinions, justifies them with reasons and consequences, expresses reservations
units.rationale: Builds on comparison and connectors to support simple argument

units.title: Going out and organising together
units.goal: Makes and reacts to suggestions, organises a joint activity and offers help
units.rationale: Social planning recycles modals, the conditional chunk and on in a cooperative task

units.title: Health, advice and obligation
units.goal: Describes symptoms and physical states, gives advice and warnings, and expresses obligation and prohibition
units.rationale: Health is a key A2 survival domain and the natural context for advice and obligation

units.title: The telephone and managing conversation
units.goal: Makes phone calls, opens and closes conversations, interrupts politely, checks understanding, paraphrases and asks for details
units.rationale: Interaction management is listed as key discourse content at A2; phone calls make it necessary without visual support

units.title: Places, customs and feelings
units.goal: Presents a country or town, its customs and environment, and expresses feelings
units.rationale: Moves from describing one's surroundings to describing a culture and personal reactions

units.title: Services, problems and notices
units.goal: Complains and asks for solutions, follows instructions and rules, handles money conventions, reads nominalised notices
units.rationale: Service encounters with problems are a typical A2 need for travellers and residents

units.title: Grammar consolidation: negation, prepositions, time
units.goal: Uses ne … plus / rien / personne, verbs and adjectives with à/de, sans + infinitive, frequency adverbs and time expressions
units.rationale: Gathers the remaining A2 grammar points that refine sentences already being produced

units.title: Study, presentations and media
units.goal: Talks about education, gives a short presentation, reads the press and follows simple media
units.rationale: Integrates A2 into the reception text types the Inventaire lists for the press and broadcast media

units.title: Writing and mediation
units.goal: Writes formal emails, blog posts and messages to shops, and relays simple information between languages
units.rationale: Written production and mediation need explicit tasks that the Inventaire does not itemise

units.title: Strategies and varieties of French
units.goal: Guesses words from context, scans texts, recognises regional varieties and spoken features
units.rationale: Strategies and variety awareness prepare learners for unadapted input beyond the course

tracks.title: Children 8–12 who can already read and write
tracks.learner: Children aged 8–12 who read and write confidently in their first language (English or another alphabetic language, or Chinese with pinyin); 2–3 lessons a week at school or in a club; short attention spans, motivated by games, songs and stories
tracks.goal: Reach A1 and a selected part of A2: talk about themselves, family, school, likes, food and holidays; read and write short texts; tell a simple story in the past
tracks.entry: Starts with classroom language, greetings and the sounds of French through songs and sound games before any grammar; the alphabet and sound–spelling links come early because children can already read
tracks.adapt: No grammar terminology in instructions; grammar points are taught as patterns and chunks. Adult-oriented KCs (work, money, formal letters, complaints, the press, telephone etiquette) are left out; topics are re-skinned for school, pets, games and family. Mastery mainly via match, listen-comprehend, role-play and picture-based situated production. Required prerequisites of selected A2 points are pulled into the stage automatically.

stages.title: Hello and the sounds of French
Me, my family and my things
Describing, my day and what I like
What I did; reading and writing little texts

tracks.title: Teenagers and students (school or DELF A1–A2)
tracks.learner: Learners aged 13–20 in secondary school or university, studying French as a subject or for the DELF A1/A2 exams; comfortable with grammar explanations; 3–4 hours a week
tracks.goal: Cover the whole A1–A2 course backbone with exam-type tasks in all four skills; be able to present a school topic and argue simply
tracks.entry: Follows the main path from the grammar-free first unit, but brings the school and presentation KCs forward to the start of A2 because classes and exams require them
tracks.adapt: Grammar terminology is allowed. Mastery uses exam-like item types (read-comprehend, listen-comprehend, situated-production-written, role-play) alongside form-fill and transform. The children's classroom-language supplement is dropped; everything else in the path is kept.

stages.title: Town, plans, the past and everyday texts
School life, stories and the future

tracks.title: Adults: everyday life and travel
tracks.learner: Adults (18+) learning for travel, a stay in a francophone country or social contact; limited time (1–3 hours a week), want usable language quickly and dislike long grammar explanations
tracks.goal: Handle travel and everyday transactions at A1, then solve problems (phone, complaints, health, services) and hold everyday conversations at A2
tracks.entry: Survival chunks first (greetings, spelling, numbers, personal details), then the transactional KCs of travel (shopping, restaurant, directions, transport, notices) are pulled forward before the rest of A1; each pulled KC brings its required prerequisites with it
tracks.adapt: Grammar is introduced when a transaction needs it; mastery stresses role-play, listen-comprehend and real-document reading. School-oriented KCs, literary reading, the press, A2 pronoun subtleties (possessive/demonstrative/indefinite pronouns) and il faut que + subjunctive are left out of the core track.

stages.title: Survival: greet, spell, count, give your details
Getting around: shops, food, directions, time and transport
Talking about yourself and your day

kcs.label: Greeting people and saying goodbye
kcs.description: Fixed expressions to open and close an encounter: a greeting chosen by time of day and relationship, the standard 'how are you' exchange, and leave-taking formulas. In France a greeting is expected before any request, even to a shop assistant or bus driver; at A1 these are learned as whole chunks.
forms: Bonjour (all day until evening) / Bonsoir (evening) / Salut (friends)
Bonjour, madame / monsieur (polite, no surname needed)
Ça va ? – Ça va bien, merci. Et toi ? / Comment allez-vous ? – Très bien, merci. Et vous ?
Au revoir. / À bientôt. / À demain. / À plus tard. / Salut ! (informal goodbye)
Bonne journée ! / Bonne soirée ! / Bonne nuit ! (only when going to bed)

examples.fr: Bonjour, madame. Un café, s'il vous plaît.
examples.en: Good morning (madam). A coffee, please.

examples.fr: Salut Léa, ça va ? – Oui, ça va, et toi ?
examples.en: Hi Léa, how are things? – Fine, and you?

examples.fr: Au revoir, monsieur, bonne journée !
examples.en: Goodbye (sir), have a nice day!

mastery: Chooses bonjour, bonsoir or salut correctly from a picture showing time of day and the relationship between speakers
Answers Ça va ? and Comment allez-vous ? with a matching register and returns the question
Opens and closes a short service encounter (shop, reception) with a greeting, madame/monsieur and a leave-taking formula
commonErrors: (EN) Saying Bonne nuit as a greeting in the evening (it is only said at bedtime); bonsoir is the evening greeting
(EN) Starting a request without bonjour, which sounds abrupt in France
(EN) Using salut with a stranger or a shop assistant
(EN) Adding a surname after madame/monsieur in a shop (Bonjour, madame is enough)
boundaries: Choosing tu or vous is kt:fr-soc-tu-vous; thanking and apologising are kt:fr-fn-thanks-apologies.
Variety note: in Québec bonjour is also used as a goodbye, and bonne nuit can be heard more widely; this KC describes metropolitan France.

primitives.binding: Turn-by-turn greeting at a bakery counter and with a friend; the clerk branches if no bonjour is given; checks greeting choice by time and relationship
Same encounter with a neighbour, a teacher and a classmate; learner adjusts salut/bonjour and ça va/comment allez-vous

kcs.label: Tu or vous: choosing the form of address
kcs.description: French has two 'you' forms for one person: tu for family, friends, children and peers of the same age group in informal settings; vous for strangers, older people, customers and anyone in a formal relation. Vous is also always the plural. The choice affects verb endings and set phrases (et toi ? / et vous ?, s'il te plaît / s'il vous plaît).
forms: tu + verb (tu es, tu as, tu veux) — one familiar person
vous + verb (vous êtes, vous avez, vous voulez) — one person politely, or several people
s'il te plaît / s'il vous plaît; et toi ? / et vous ?
On se tutoie ? / On peut se tutoyer ? (proposing tu)

examples.fr: Vous êtes Madame Martin ? – Oui, c'est moi.
examples.en: Are you Mrs Martin? – Yes, that's me.

examples.fr: Tu as quel âge, Hugo ?
examples.en: How old are you, Hugo?

examples.fr: On se tutoie ? – Oui, bien sûr !
examples.en: Shall we say tu? – Yes, of course!

mastery: Says whether tu or vous fits a described relationship (classmate, shop assistant, teacher, grandmother, two friends)
Rewrites a short request from tu to vous, changing the verb ending and s'il te plaît / s'il vous plaît
Keeps one form consistently through a role-play and switches when the partner proposes tutoiement
commonErrors: (EN) Using tu with a stranger or a shop assistant
(EN) Mixing tu and vous in one exchange (Vous êtes français ? Et toi ?)
(EN) Thinking vous is only plural and treating it as rude to use it with one person
(ZH) Treating vous like 您 only for elders; in French it is also the default with any adult stranger
boundaries: Only the choice of address; verb forms are learned with each verb.
Practice varies: workplaces, young people and Québec use tu more readily; when unsure, start with vous and wait to be offered tu.

primitives.binding: Six relationship cards (boss, neighbour child, waiter, cousin, two customers, new classmate); learner picks tu/vous and sees what the other person would feel
Short story of a learner who says tu to a pharmacist; learner explains the reaction and rewrites the request

kcs.label: Thanking, apologising and responding
kcs.description: Formulas for thanking and apologising and the usual replies. French distinguishes pardon (small slips, getting past someone, asking someone to repeat) from excusez-moi / désolé(e) (apologising for a real inconvenience).
forms: Merci. / Merci beaucoup. / Merci bien.
De rien. / Je vous en prie. / Avec plaisir.
Pardon ! (bumping into someone, getting past)
Excusez-moi / Excuse-moi
Je suis désolé(e). / Désolé(e).
Ce n'est pas grave.

examples.fr: Merci beaucoup, madame ! – Je vous en prie.
examples.en: Thank you very much! – You're welcome.

examples.fr: Pardon, je peux passer ?
examples.en: Sorry, can I get past?

examples.fr: Je suis désolée, je suis en retard. – Ce n'est pas grave.
examples.en: I'm sorry, I'm late. – It doesn't matter.

mastery: Matches merci, pardon, désolé(e) and de rien to short pictured situations
Gives the right reply to merci (de rien / je vous en prie) and to an apology (ce n'est pas grave)
Thanks and apologises appropriately in a role-play at a shop or on public transport
commonErrors: (EN) Answering merci with *Bienvenue (a calque of "you're welcome"; in France say de rien / je vous en prie)
(EN) Writing désolé without the -e when the speaker is a woman
(EN) Using pardon for a serious apology
boundaries: Inviting and accepting/refusing are kt:fr-fn-invitations; asking someone to repeat is kt:fr-str-repair.
Variety note: in Québec bienvenue is the normal reply to merci; in France it is understood but not used.

primitives.binding: Three micro-scenes (holding a door, stepping on a foot, arriving late); learner picks thanks/apology and the partner's reply branches
Judge eight lines: is pardon / excusez-moi / désolé(e) acceptable here? Classify by situation, then write one of each

kcs.label: Approaching someone and asking for something
kcs.description: How to get a stranger's attention and make a minimal request: an opener (excusez-moi, s'il vous plaît, pardon, madame/monsieur) followed by a noun or short question. This lets a learner function before knowing any verbs.
forms: Excusez-moi, madame / monsieur…
S'il vous plaît ! (calling a waiter)
Pardon, … ?
[noun], s'il vous plaît ? (La gare, s'il vous plaît ?)
Vous avez … ? / Il y a … ?

examples.fr: Excusez-moi, monsieur, la gare, s'il vous plaît ?
examples.en: Excuse me, where is the station, please?

examples.fr: S'il vous plaît ! L'addition, s'il vous plaît.
examples.en: Excuse me! The bill, please.

mastery: Identifies which openers are polite ways to stop a stranger in the street
Builds an opener + noun + s'il vous plaît request for a pictured need (toilets, metro, bill)
Stops a passer-by in a role-play and obtains one piece of information
commonErrors: (EN) Saying *Excuse-moi to a stranger (tu form) instead of excusez-moi
(EN) Calling a waiter garçon !, which is now considered rude; use s'il vous plaît or monsieur/madame
boundaries: Asking for directions in full is kt:fr-fn-directions; asking for information in general is kt:fr-fn-ask-information.

primitives.binding: Stop a passer-by, a waiter and a ticket clerk; branches when the opener is missing or too familiar
Walk through a station: at each point retrieve the opener plus the noun needed

kcs.label: Saying you don't understand and asking for repetition
kcs.term: Je ne comprends pas. Vous pouvez répéter ?
kcs.description: Chunks that keep a conversation going when understanding breaks down: saying you do not understand, asking for repetition or slower speech, and asking what a word means. Taught as fixed phrases at the very start.
forms: Je ne comprends pas.
Pardon ? / Comment ?
Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ? / Tu peux répéter ?
Plus lentement, s'il vous plaît.
Qu'est-ce que ça veut dire, « … » ?
Comment on dit … en français ?

examples.fr: Pardon, je ne comprends pas. Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?
examples.en: Sorry, I don't understand. Can you repeat, please?

examples.fr: Qu'est-ce que ça veut dire, « boulangerie » ?
examples.en: What does "boulangerie" mean?

mastery: Picks the right repair phrase for a described problem (too fast, unknown word, did not hear)
Produces the phrases from memory with correct ne … pas and s'il vous plaît
Uses at least one repair move when an audio prompt is too fast, then completes the task
commonErrors: (EN) *Je ne comprends (missing pas) or *Je comprends pas in writing
(EN) Saying *Répétez ! alone, which sounds like an order; add s'il vous plaît or use vous pouvez
boundaries: Spelling a word on request is kt:fr-orth-spelling-aloud; polite interruption and checking understanding at A2 are kt:fr-dis-interrupt and kt:fr-dis-check-understanding.

primitives.binding: A partner speaks too fast or uses an unknown word at set points; the learner must stop them with the right phrase before continuing
Learner says the repair phrase for each problem card before seeing it; first attempts kept

kcs.label: The French alphabet and letter names
kcs.description: French uses the same 26 Latin letters as English, but their names differ (e.g. e, g, i, j, r, u, w, y). Letter names are needed to spell names, emails and addresses aloud and to understand spelled words.
forms: a [a], b [be], c [se], d [de], e [ə], f [ɛf], g [ʒe], h [aʃ], i [i], j [ʒi], k [ka], l [ɛl], m [ɛm], n [ɛn], o [o], p [pe], q [ky], r [ɛʁ], s [ɛs], t [te], u [y], v [ve], w [dubləve], x [iks], y [igʁɛk], z [zɛd]
majuscule / minuscule
deux « l » / double « l » (both heard)

examples.fr: Martin : M-A-R-T-I-N.
examples.en: Martin: M-A-R-T-I-N.

examples.fr: « Gilles », ça s'écrit G-I-deux L-E-S.
examples.en: "Gilles" is spelled G-I-double L-E-S.

mastery: Hears a letter name and selects the letter, including the confusable pairs e/i, g/j, u/ou
Recites and writes the alphabet in order in upper and lower case
Writes down a 4–8 letter word or name spelled aloud at normal speed
commonErrors: (EN) Reading e as English "ee" and i as "eye"
(EN) Swapping g [ʒe] and j [ʒi] (English names are the other way round)
(EN) Saying u as English "you"; French u is [y]
(ZH) Reading letters with pinyin values (e.g. e as pinyin e)
boundaries: Letter names only; how letters sound inside words is kt:fr-orth-sound-spelling; accents are kt:fr-orth-accents.

primitives.binding: Letter-name pairs e/i, g/j, u/ou-sound, b/v from the fr-alphabet sound-grid pack; checks the learner can hear and say each name distinctly
Hear spelled surnames and city names and type them into a form field; checks each letter

kcs.label: Spelling names and words aloud, with accents
kcs.description: Spelling and understanding spelled words in a real exchange: asking how something is written, spelling a surname, an email address or a street, and naming accents and double letters.
forms: Ça s'écrit comment ? / Vous pouvez épeler, s'il vous plaît ?
e accent aigu (é), e accent grave (è), c cédille (ç)
deux « s », tiret (-), apostrophe
arobase (@), point (.), tiret bas (_)

examples.fr: Votre nom, ça s'écrit comment ? – D-U-P-O-N-T.
examples.en: How do you spell your name? – D-U-P-O-N-T.

examples.fr: Mon mail, c'est lea point roux arobase exemple point fr.
examples.en: My email is lea dot roux at exemple dot fr.

mastery: Identifies the spelled word among written options, including accented letters
Spells own name, street and email aloud, naming accents and symbols
Completes a booking form by asking for and checking the spelling of a name
commonErrors: (EN) Forgetting to say the accent (é spelled just "e")
(EN) Saying "at" for @ instead of arobase
boundaries: Requires the letter names of kt:fr-orth-alphabet; the meaning of accents is kt:fr-orth-accents.

primitives.binding: Hear a spelled name, email and postcode and type them into form slots; errors classified as letter, accent or symbol

kcs.label: Classroom language and instructions
kcs.description: Understanding the instructions of a lesson or a worksheet (écoutez, lisez, répétez, cochez, complétez) and the phrases a learner needs in class (Comment on dit … ? Je peux aller aux toilettes ?).
forms: Écoutez. Répétez. Lisez. Écrivez. Regardez le tableau.
Ouvrez / fermez vos livres. Travaillez à deux.
worksheet: Cochez. Complétez. Reliez. Soulignez. Entourez.
learner: J'ai fini. / Je peux aller aux toilettes ? / Comment on dit … en français ? / Je n'ai pas compris.

examples.fr: Ouvrez vos livres page 12 et lisez le texte.
examples.en: Open your books at page 12 and read the text.

examples.fr: Madame, comment on dit « pencil » en français ?
examples.en: Miss, how do you say "pencil" in French?

mastery: Performs ten classroom instructions given orally
Follows written worksheet instructions (cochez, reliez, complétez)
Uses three learner phrases appropriately during a lesson

(EN) Confusing écoutez and écrivez in fast speech

kcs.label: Key oral vowel contrasts
kcs.description: French vowels are tense and do not glide as English vowels do. Several contrasts carry meaning: [y] (tu) vs [u] (tout), [e] (les, été) vs [ə] (le, je), [e] vs [ɛ] (é vs è). At A1 the priority is hearing and producing tu/tout and le/les clearly.
forms: [y] vs [u]: tu – tout, rue – roue, dessus – dessous
[ə] vs [e]: le – les, de – des, je – j'ai (approx.)
[e] vs [ɛ]: été – fête, et – est (many speakers)
[i] vs [y]: si – su, dit – du
no diphthong: café [kafe], not "kafay"

examples.fr: Tu as vu la rue ?
examples.en: Did you see the street?

examples.fr: Le livre ou les livres ?
examples.en: The book or the books?

mastery: Hears one word of a minimal pair (tu/tout, le/les) and selects it
Produces tu/tout and le/les so that a listener can tell them apart
Reads a short sentence with [y] and [u] without replacing [y] by [u]
commonErrors: (EN) Pronouncing u as [u] ("too") so that tu sounds like tout and dessus like dessous
(EN) Diphthongising é and o (café as "kafay", beau as "bow")
(EN) Pronouncing le and les the same, which hides singular/plural
boundaries: Nasal vowels are kt:fr-phon-nasal-vowels; spelling of these vowels is kt:fr-orth-sound-spelling.
The [e]/[ɛ] distinction in some positions varies by region (southern France, Québec); only clear cases are tested.

primitives.binding: Minimal pairs tu/tout, rue/roue, le/les, dessus/dessous; checks discrimination first, then whether a listener can identify the learner's word
Learner records a phrase with tu/tout, writes what they said, then compares with what a listener heard

citations.locator: CEFR 2001 §5.2.1.4 Phonological competence
citations.note: L'Inventaire (§5, p. 14–15) présente des contenus clés « non exhaustifs » et ne détaille ni l'orthographe ni la prononciation (seul le scénario A2 « Partir en vacances » cite « liaisons, rythme, intonation »). Contrasts such as tu/tout and le/les carry meaning and are absent from English.

kcs.label: Nasal vowels
kcs.description: French has three to four nasal vowels in which air passes through the nose and no [n] is pronounced: [ɑ̃] (an, en), [ɔ̃] (on), [ɛ̃] (in, ain, un for many speakers). They distinguish words from each other and from oral vowels (beau/bon, vin/vent).
forms: [ɑ̃]: an, en, am, em — enfant, temps
[ɔ̃]: on, om — bon, nom
[ɛ̃]: in, im, ain, ein — vin, pain, plein; un for many speakers
oral vs nasal: beau – bon, sa – sans, fait – fin
no nasal vowel before a vowel or double n/m: bon – bonne, an – année

examples.fr: Le pain et le vin sont bons.
examples.en: The bread and the wine are good.

examples.fr: Mon enfant a cinq ans.
examples.en: My child is five years old.

mastery: Distinguishes vin/vent/vont and beau/bon when heard
Produces the three nasal vowels without adding [n] or [ŋ]
Reads aloud bon/bonne, an/année with the correct nasal or oral vowel
commonErrors: (EN) Pronouncing an [n] or [ŋ] after the vowel (bon as "bong")
(EN) Mixing [ɑ̃] and [ɔ̃] (vent/vont)
(EN) Nasalising bonne and année by analogy with bon and an
boundaries: Spelling patterns are kt:fr-orth-sound-spelling.
Many speakers in northern France merge un [œ̃] with in [ɛ̃]; Québec and Belgian French keep [œ̃] more often. The merged system is taught as standard.

primitives.binding: Three-way sets vin/vent/vont, pain/pan/pont plus oral/nasal pairs beau/bon; checks hearing then intelligible production
fr-blend pack: an, on, ain as one box; learner blends and then spells bon/bonne

citations.locator: CEFR 2001 §5.2.1.4 Phonological competence
citations.note: L'Inventaire (§5, p. 14–15) présente des contenus clés « non exhaustifs » et ne détaille ni l'orthographe ni la prononciation (seul le scénario A2 « Partir en vacances » cite « liaisons, rythme, intonation »). Nasal vowels distinguish words (beau/bon, vin/vent) and do not exist as phonemes in English.

kcs.label: French r and other consonants
kcs.description: Consonant features that most affect intelligibility for English speakers: the uvular French r [ʁ], unaspirated p t k, the sounds [ʒ] (je, rouge) and [ɲ] (montagne), silent h, and the fact that final consonants are often not pronounced.
forms: [ʁ] produced at the back of the mouth: rue, Paris, merci
p t k without a puff of air: papa, tu, café
[ʒ]: je, jour, rouge, gentil
[ɲ]: montagne, gagner
h is never pronounced: hôtel [otɛl], homme [ɔm]

examples.fr: Je voudrais un croissant, merci.
examples.en: I'd like a croissant, thank you.

examples.fr: L'hôtel est à la montagne.
examples.en: The hotel is in the mountains.

mastery: Recognises French r and [ʒ] in words heard (rouge, jour)
Produces r and [ʒ] intelligibly in short words and in merci, Paris, bonjour
Reads hôtel, homme, heure without an [h]
commonErrors: (EN) Pronouncing an English r or no r at all (merci as "mehsi")
(EN) Pronouncing h in hôtel, haricot
(EN) Using [dʒ] for j (je as "juh")
(ZH) Replacing [ʒ] by pinyin r or zh
boundaries: Which final consonants are silent is kt:fr-orth-silent-letters; linking is kt:fr-phon-linking.
A rolled r is heard in some regions, in Québec and in singing; it is understood but the uvular r is the reference.

primitives.binding: Pairs with and without [ʁ] (gars/gare, pas/part) and [ʒ]/[ʃ] (jeu/cheveux onset); checks listener can recognise the target
Record bonjour, merci, Paris; self-check the r and compare with a model

kcs.label: Accents and diacritics
kcs.description: French marks some letters with accents: é (accent aigu), è à ù (accent grave), ê â î ô û (accent circonflexe), ë ï (tréma) and ç (cédille). Accents on e change its sound; on other letters they mostly distinguish words (a/à, ou/où, du/dû) or follow history. Accents are part of correct spelling, including on capitals in careful writing.
forms: é = [e]: été, café
è / ê = [ɛ]: père, fête
ç = [s] before a, o, u: ça, garçon, reçu
à, où, là distinguish words: il a / à Paris; ou / où; la / là
ë, ï: Noël, maïs (vowels said separately)

examples.fr: Il a un garçon. Ils habitent à Nice.
examples.en: He has a boy. They live in Nice.

examples.fr: Tu vas où ? – Là-bas, au café.
examples.en: Where are you going? – Over there, to the café.

mastery: Reads é, è/ê and e without accent with the expected sound in common words
Chooses a/à, ou/où, la/là in gapped sentences
Writes common A1 words with their accents and ç (français, garçon, très, à bientôt)
commonErrors: (EN) Leaving accents out as optional decoration
(EN) Confusing accent aigu and grave (*trés, *pére)
(EN) Writing *francais or *garcon without ç
boundaries: Letter combinations without accents are kt:fr-orth-sound-spelling.
On keyboards, accents may be typed via a French layout or long-press; that is not tested here.

primitives.binding: Sentence pairs that differ only by a/à or ou/où; learner judges the meaning, forced to look at the accent
fr-alphabet pack: é/è/e and ç cells; learner hears a word and selects the accented letter

Accents change pronunciation and sometimes meaning (a/à, ou/où) and must be read and written from the start.

kcs.label: Reading French letter groups
kcs.description: French spelling is regular in the reading direction once letter groups are known: several letters often spell one sound (ou, oi, au/eau, ai, an/en, on, in/ain, eu, ch, gn, qu, ph) and some letters change value by context (c and g before e/i, s between vowels). These rules let learners read unknown words aloud.
forms: ou [u]: vous; oi [wa]: moi; au/eau [o]: eau, beau; ai/ei [ɛ]: lait, neige; eu/œu [ø]/[œ]: deux, sœur
ch [ʃ]: chat; gn [ɲ]: ligne; qu [k]: qui; ph [f]: photo
c = [s] before e, i (ici), [k] elsewhere (café); g = [ʒ] before e, i (rouge), [g] elsewhere (gare)
s between vowels = [z]: maison; ss = [s]: poisson
ill often [j]: fille, travailler (but ville, mille [il])

examples.fr: Le chat boit de l'eau.
examples.en: The cat drinks water.

examples.fr: Ma sœur a deux poissons à la maison.
examples.en: My sister has two fish at home.

mastery: Matches written letter groups (ou, oi, eau, ch, gn) to the sound heard
Reads aloud unfamiliar regular words (moineau, chapeau, poisson/poison)
Spells regular words dictated as single words using the right letter group
commonErrors: (EN) Reading oi as in "boil"
(EN) Reading ch as [tʃ] ("church")
(EN) Reading poison and poisson the same (s vs ss)
(EN) Pronouncing the letters of eau separately
boundaries: Nasal-vowel spellings are listed in kt:fr-phon-nasal-vowels; silent endings are kt:fr-orth-silent-letters.
Irregular words (femme, monsieur, oignon, fils) are learned individually; see REVIEW.md.

primitives.binding: fr-blend pack: blend chapeau, poisson, maison from grapheme boxes (ch, eau, ss, ai, on), then spell them back
Start from words the learner already says (bonjour, merci, chocolat) and link each grapheme to the sound

kcs.label: Silent letters and silent endings
kcs.description: Many written letters are not pronounced: final -e, most final consonants (-s, -t, -d, -x, -z, -p), and the verb ending -ent. Because plural -s and the person endings of -er verbs are usually silent, singular and plural or je/tu/il/ils forms often sound the same and are distinguished only in writing or by the article/pronoun. Final c, r, f, l are often pronounced (the 'careful' rule).
forms: final -e silent: table, porte
final -s, -t, -d, -x silent: les amis, petit, grand, deux
verb -ent silent: ils parlent = il parle (sound)
often pronounced: final c, r, f, l (sac, bonjour, neuf, sel) — but -er verbs and many -er nouns: parler, boulanger
plural heard on the article: le livre / les livres

examples.fr: Ils parlent anglais.
examples.en: They speak English.

examples.fr: Les petits chats sont gris.
examples.en: The little cats are grey.

mastery: Crosses out silent letters in a short written text
Reads aloud word lists with silent endings correctly (petit, grand, ils mangent)
Writes dictated sentences with the silent plural and verb endings
commonErrors: (EN) Pronouncing -ent in ils parlent
(EN) Pronouncing final -s and -t (les amis as "lez amees")
(EN) Omitting plural -s in writing because it is not heard
boundaries: When a silent final consonant is pronounced before a vowel is kt:fr-phon-linking.
Number words (six, dix, huit, cinq, sept) have special rules; see kt:fr-lex-numbers-0-69.

primitives.binding: fr-blend pack silent boxes (t:0, s:0): learner builds petit, grand, parlent and sees silent letters in dashed boxes
Hear il parle / ils parlent: decide singular or plural only from what is audible (pronoun, liaison), then check with the written form

kcs.label: Elision, liaison and linking
kcs.description: French joins words within a group. Elision drops a vowel before a vowel sound and is written with an apostrophe (je → j', le/la → l', de → d', ne → n', que → qu', si + il → s'il). Liaison pronounces a normally silent final consonant before a vowel in fixed contexts (les‿amis [lezami], vous‿avez, un‿enfant). Enchaînement carries a pronounced final consonant onto the next vowel (il‿a).
forms: elision: j'aime, l'ami, l'école, je n'ai pas, qu'est-ce que, s'il vous plaît
obligatory liaison: les‿amis, vous‿êtes, nous‿avons, un‿enfant, deux‿ans, très‿important
no liaison after et: et | il; no elision or liaison before aspirated h: le héros, les | haricots
enchaînement: il‿arrive, avec‿elle

examples.fr: J'habite à Lyon avec mes amis.
examples.en: I live in Lyon with my friends.

examples.fr: Vous avez deux enfants ? – Oui, ils ont six et huit ans.
examples.en: Do you have two children? – Yes, they are six and eight.

mastery: Hears where liaison occurs in a short phrase and marks it
Writes elided forms correctly (j'aime, l'hôtel, n'est)
Reads A1 phrases with obligatory liaisons (vous‿êtes, les‿enfants) and no liaison after et
commonErrors: (EN) Writing *je aime, *le ami (no elision)
(EN) Missing obligatory liaison (vous | avez), so the phrase sounds broken
(EN) Making liaison after et
(EN) Not recognising mots heard with liaison (les‿amis heard as "lézamis")
boundaries: Only obligatory and forbidden A1 cases; optional liaisons belong to higher levels.
Silent letters in isolation are kt:fr-orth-silent-letters.
kcs.placementNote: Placed in A1: elision is needed in writing from the first sentence (j'habite, je m'appelle); the Inventaire names liaison only in the A2 scenario.

primitives.binding: Learner writes a short dictated phrase, then aligns it with the text to see where liaison and elision hid the word boundaries
Mark liaisons and links in a model phrase, shadow it, compare pauses

kcs.label: Rhythm, final stress and question intonation
kcs.description: French has even syllables with stress on the last syllable of each word group, not on a fixed syllable of each word. Yes/no questions are often asked by intonation alone, with the voice rising at the end; statements fall at the end.
forms: groupe rythmique: stress on the last syllable — Je m'appelle Pauline.
syllables of equal length: ca-fé, a-ni-mal (not "ANimal")
rising question: Tu viens ? ↗
falling statement: Tu viens. ↘
falling wh-question: Tu habites où ? (variable)

examples.fr: Tu as faim ? ↗ – Oui, j'ai faim. ↘
examples.en: Are you hungry? – Yes, I'm hungry.

examples.fr: Elle s'appelle Juliette.
examples.en: Her name is Juliette.

mastery: Hears whether a short utterance is a question or a statement from intonation only
Reads a question with rising intonation and a statement with falling intonation
Repeats names and phrases with final stress (Ju-li-ETTE, ca-fé)
commonErrors: (EN) Stressing the first syllable of international words (ANimal, CHOcolat)
(EN) Asking a question with flat or falling intonation so it sounds like a statement
boundaries: Question forms are kt:fr-g-yes-no-questions.
Intonation of wh-questions varies a lot in speech; it is not tested here.
kcs.placementNote: Placed in A1: intonation questions are used from the first unit; the Inventaire names rhythm and intonation only in the A2 scenario.

primitives.binding: Learner draws or selects rising vs falling contours for heard utterances, then speaks to match a given contour
Shadow two-group sentences, marking the stressed last syllable of each group

kcs.label: Subject pronouns
kcs.description: French verbs need a subject: je, tu, il, elle, on, nous, vous, ils, elles. Il/elle and ils/elles follow grammatical gender, so they can mean 'it' and 'they' for things. Ils is used for any group that contains a masculine noun. Je becomes j' before a vowel.
forms: je (j') / tu / il / elle / on
nous / vous / ils / elles
il = he or it (masculine noun); elle = she or it (feminine noun)
ils = mixed or masculine group; elles = all-feminine group

examples.fr: La voiture ? Elle est dans la rue.
examples.en: The car? It's in the street.

examples.fr: Paul et Marie ? Ils sont au travail.
examples.en: Paul and Marie? They're at work.

mastery: Chooses the subject pronoun that replaces a given noun (la table → elle, mes amis → ils)
Fills subject gaps in a short text, including ils for mixed groups
Talks about a family photo using il/elle/ils/elles consistently
commonErrors: (EN) Using il only for people and *ça for masculine things in every case
(EN) Using elles for a mixed group
(ZH) Dropping the subject as in Chinese (*Suis étudiant)
boundaries: Tonic pronouns (moi, toi…) are kt:fr-g-tonic-pronouns; on is kt:fr-g-on; tu/vous choice is kt:fr-soc-tu-vous.

primitives.binding: Short text about people and objects; learner links each il/elle/ils to its noun, including grammatical-gender things
Hear il est grand / elle est grande about a pictured object; decide which object is meant

kcs.label: Être in the present
kcs.description: Être ('to be') is irregular and the most frequent verb: je suis, tu es, il/elle/on est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont. It links a subject to a nationality, job, quality or place, and is the auxiliary of some past-tense verbs later.
forms: je suis, tu es, il/elle/on est
nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont
être + nationality/job without article: Je suis professeur.
être + adjective: Il est content.
être + à/de + place: Je suis de Montréal. Il est à Paris.

examples.fr: Je suis étudiante. Je suis de Dublin.
examples.en: I'm a student. I'm from Dublin.

examples.fr: Vous êtes français ? – Non, nous sommes belges.
examples.en: Are you French? – No, we're Belgian.

mastery: Selects the right form of être for each subject
Writes all six forms from memory
Introduces self and a friend with être (nationality, job, city)
commonErrors: (EN) Using an article before a job (*Je suis un professeur)
(EN) Confusing est and et (same sound) in writing
(EN) *Je suis 20 ans (age uses avoir)
boundaries: Age and hunger use avoir: kt:fr-g-avoir-present. C'est vs il est is kt:fr-g-cest-presentatives.

primitives.binding: Fill the être table, then apply it to new subjects in a short dialogue; each choice shows the person rule

kcs.label: Avoir in the present and expressions with avoir
kcs.description: Avoir ('to have') is irregular: j'ai, tu as, il/elle/on a, nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont. French uses avoir where English uses 'be' for age and several physical states (avoir … ans, avoir faim/soif/chaud/froid/peur).
forms: j'ai, tu as, il/elle/on a, nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont
avoir + âge: J'ai vingt ans.
avoir faim / soif / chaud / froid / sommeil / peur
Tu as quel âge ? / Quel âge avez-vous ?
ils ont [ɔ̃] vs ils sont [sɔ̃]

examples.fr: J'ai dix-neuf ans et j'ai un frère.
examples.en: I'm nineteen and I have a brother.

examples.fr: Vous avez faim ? – Non, mais j'ai soif.

mastery: Distinguishes ils ont / ils sont when heard
Fills in avoir forms and uses avoir for age
Answers questions about age, family and hunger/thirst in a short exchange
commonErrors: (EN) *Je suis 20 ans / *Je suis faim
(EN) Saying ils sont for ils ont (missing liaison [z] makes the difference)
(EN) *Je a (no elision to j'ai)
boundaries: Il y a (there is/are) is kt:fr-g-il-y-a; avoir as past auxiliary is kt:fr-g-pc-avoir.

kcs.label: Introducing yourself and others
kcs.description: Giving and asking for name, origin and basic identity, and introducing a third person. The chunks Je m'appelle… and Comment tu t'appelles ? are learned before the grammar of pronominal verbs.
forms: Je m'appelle … / Moi, c'est …
Comment tu t'appelles ? / Comment vous appelez-vous ? / Tu t'appelles comment ?
Je suis … / J'habite à … / Je viens de …
Je te présente … / Je vous présente … / Voici … / C'est …
Enchanté(e). / Ravi(e) de faire votre connaissance.

examples.fr: Bonjour, je m'appelle Sofia. Et toi ? – Moi, c'est Malik.

kcs.label: Countries, nationalities and languages
kcs.description: Names of countries (with their gender and article), nationality adjectives and nouns, and language names. Nationality adjectives agree in gender and are not capitalised; nationality nouns are (un Français).
forms: la France, l'Espagne, la Chine, le Canada, le Japon, les États-Unis
français / française, anglais / anglaise, chinois / chinoise, espagnol / espagnole, belge, suisse
américain / américaine, canadien / canadienne, italien / italienne
parler + language without article: Je parle anglais.
un Français / une Française (noun, capital)

kcs.label: C'est, ce sont, voici, voilà; c'est vs il est
kcs.description: Presentatives identify or point things out: c'est / ce sont + noun group, voici / voilà + noun. C'est also introduces a person by name or job with an article (c'est un médecin), while il/elle est + job or adjective has no article (il est médecin).
forms: c'est + singular noun group: C'est mon frère.
ce sont + plural: Ce sont mes parents. (c'est also heard in speech)
voici / voilà + noun: Voilà le bus !
c'est + article + noun vs il/elle est + noun without article
C'est + adjective for a general comment: C'est beau !

examples.fr: Qui est-ce ? – C'est Marc. Il est infirmier.
examples.en: Who is it? – It's Marc. He's a nurse.

examples.fr: Voilà vos clés, madame.
examples.en: Here are your keys, madam.

mastery: Chooses c'est or il est in gapped sentences about people
Transforms il est professeur ↔ c'est un professeur
Presents objects and people in a photo using c'est, ce sont and voilà
commonErrors: (EN) *Il est un médecin / *C'est médecin
(EN) *C'est mes amis in writing (ce sont in standard written French)
boundaries: Qui est-ce ? / Qu'est-ce que c'est ? are kt:fr-g-qui-est-ce; ça is kt:fr-g-ca.

primitives.binding: Same person or object; learner chooses c'est un… or il est… depending on whether identifying or describing, and sees the alternative
Judge eight sentences with c'est/il est and articles; classify the error, then write two correct ones

kcs.label: Asking what or who something is
kcs.description: Two fixed identification questions: Qui est-ce ? (who is it?) for people and Qu'est-ce que c'est ? (what is it?) for things. Speech also uses C'est qui ? and C'est quoi ?.

Qu'est-ce que c'est ? – C'est un/une …
Spoken: C'est qui ? / C'est quoi ?
Plural answer: Ce sont des …

examples.fr: Qu'est-ce que c'est ? – C'est un tire-bouchon.
examples.en: What is it? – It's a corkscrew.

examples.fr: Qui est-ce, sur la photo ? – C'est ma grand-mère.
examples.en: Who is that in the photo? – It's my grandmother.

mastery: Chooses the right question for a person or an object picture
Asks and answers about six unknown objects
Identifies people in a photo for a partner using the questions

(EN) Using qui est-ce for objects
boundaries: Other question words are kt:fr-g-question-words.

kcs.label: Stressed (tonic) pronouns
kcs.description: Moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles are used alone, for emphasis, after prepositions and after c'est: Moi, je…; Et toi ?; avec lui; chez eux; C'est moi.
forms: moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles
alone / in short answers: Et toi ? – Moi aussi. / Moi non plus.
emphasis: Moi, je suis canadien.
after prepositions: avec moi, pour toi, chez lui
after c'est: C'est moi.

examples.fr: Moi, j'aime le thé. Et toi ? – Moi aussi !
examples.en: I like tea. What about you? – Me too!

examples.fr: Tu viens avec nous chez eux ?
examples.en: Are you coming with us to their place?

mastery: Chooses the tonic pronoun after avec, chez, pour and c'est
Answers Moi aussi / Moi non plus correctly to positive and negative statements
Uses moi/toi for contrast when introducing people
commonErrors: (EN) *avec je / *pour il (subject pronoun after a preposition)
(EN) Answering a negative statement with *Moi aussi instead of Moi non plus
(EN) *C'est je
boundaries: Object pronouns (le, lui as indirect object) are kt:fr-g-direct-object-pronouns and kt:fr-g-indirect-object-pronouns.

primitives.binding: Reply cards: agree with a positive or a negative statement (moi aussi / moi non plus / pas moi / moi si)
Sentences with avec lui / avec elle / chez eux; learner picks which pictured person is meant

kcs.label: Numbers 0–69
kcs.description: Cardinal numbers up to 69: the irregular 0–16, the regular pattern dix-sept to dix-neuf, tens (vingt, trente, quarante, cinquante, soixante) with et un for 21–61 and hyphens elsewhere. Some final consonants change with the next word (six, dix, huit, cinq).
forms: zéro, un, deux, trois, quatre, cinq, six, sept, huit, neuf, dix
onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze, seize; dix-sept, dix-huit, dix-neuf
vingt, trente, quarante, cinquante, soixante
vingt et un, trente et un … soixante et un; vingt-deux, trente-cinq …
six/dix: [sis] alone, [si] before a consonant (six livres), [siz] before a vowel (six ans)

examples.fr: J'ai vingt-trois ans.
examples.en: I'm twenty-three.

examples.fr: Le bus numéro quarante et un arrive.
examples.en: The number forty-one bus is coming.

mastery: Writes digits for numbers 0–69 heard in random order
Says and writes numbers with correct et un and hyphens
Exchanges ages and room or bus numbers in a short dialogue
commonErrors: (EN) Confusing douze/treize/seize
(EN) *vingt-un instead of vingt et un
(EN) Pronouncing the x of six and dix as [ks]
boundaries: 70 and above are kt:fr-lex-numbers-70-plus; telling the time is kt:fr-fn-telling-time; prices are kt:fr-fn-shopping.

primitives.binding: Hear ages, room and bus numbers in short announcements; write digits in slots; errors grouped by number range
Digit card → say the number aloud before the audio reveal; first attempt kept

kcs.label: Numbers from 70 to 1 000 000 and their regional variants
kcs.description: From 70 standard French counts in twenties: soixante-dix (60+10), quatre-vingts (4×20), quatre-vingt-dix (4×20+10). Then cent, mille, million. Belgium and Switzerland use septante and nonante (and Switzerland often huitante), which are easier but must be recognised.
forms: 70 soixante-dix, 71 soixante et onze, 72 soixante-douze … 79 soixante-dix-neuf
80 quatre-vingts, 81 quatre-vingt-un, 90 quatre-vingt-dix, 99 quatre-vingt-dix-neuf
100 cent, 200 deux cents, 250 deux cent cinquante; 1000 mille (invariable), 2026 deux mille vingt-six
un million (d'euros)
Belgium/Switzerland: septante (70), nonante (90); Switzerland (some cantons): huitante (80)

examples.fr: Le billet coûte quatre-vingt-quinze euros.
examples.en: The ticket costs ninety-five euros.

examples.fr: Mon numéro, c'est le zéro six, soixante-dix-huit, quatre-vingt-deux…
examples.en: My number is 06 78 82…

mastery: Writes digits for numbers 70–99 heard in random order
Converts soixante-dix-sept ↔ 77 and recognises septante-sept as the same number
Notes a French phone number read in pairs of digits
commonErrors: (EN) Writing 60+17 as 6017 when taking dictation of soixante-dix-sept
(EN) Confusing quatre-vingts (80) and quatre-vingt-dix (90)
(EN) Writing *mille with -s or *quatre-vingt without -s at 80
boundaries: Phone numbers are read in pairs in France; this KC covers the numbers, not number-reading conventions of other countries.
Variety: septante/nonante are standard in Belgium and Switzerland; Québec uses the France forms.

primitives.binding: Map spoken soixante-dix-huit to 60+18 and to 78, then to Belgian septante-huit; estimate, compute, then say
French phone numbers and prices dictated in pairs; learner fills slots and reviews errors by range (70s, 90s)

kcs.label: Asking for and giving personal information
kcs.description: Exchanging the details of a simple form: name, age, address, phone, nationality, job, family situation (état civil). Covers both asking (tu/vous) and answering briefly.
forms: Tu as quel âge ? / Quel âge avez-vous ?
Tu habites où ? / Où habitez-vous ? – J'habite (au) 12, rue …
Quelle est votre adresse ? / votre numéro de téléphone ?
Vous êtes marié(e) ? – Je suis célibataire / marié(e) / divorcé(e) / pacsé(e).

examples.fr: Vous habitez où ? – J'habite au 8, rue des Lilas, à Tours.

examples.fr: Tu as des frères et sœurs ? – Oui, j'ai une sœur.
examples.en: Do you have brothers and sisters? – Yes, I have a sister.

mastery: Understands spoken questions about identity, address, age and job and picks the matching answer
Writes answers to eight personal questions
Conducts a registration interview with vous and records the answers
commonErrors: (EN) Putting the number after the street name (rue des Lilas 8)
(EN) *Je suis 30 ans
(EN) Answering Qu'est-ce que vous faites ? about current activity instead of job

kcs.label: Family and social relations
kcs.description: Words for family members and close relations, with gender pairs, plus words for friends and partners. Used with possessive determiners to talk about one's family.
forms: le père / la mère, les parents
le frère / la sœur, le fils / la fille, les enfants
le grand-père / la grand-mère, l'oncle / la tante, le cousin / la cousine
le mari / la femme, le copain / la copine, un(e) ami(e)
beau-père, belle-mère (step- and in-law)
être marié(e) avec, avoir … enfants

examples.en: My mother has two sisters, so I have two aunts.

examples.fr: Voici mon cousin Hugo et sa copine.

kcs.label: Yes/no questions: intonation, est-ce que, inversion
kcs.description: Three ways to ask a yes/no question: rising intonation on a statement (Tu viens ?), est-ce que + statement (Est-ce que tu viens ?), and subject–verb inversion (Viens-tu ?, Pourriez-vous… ?). At A1 intonation and est-ce que are produced; inversion is recognised and used in fixed polite forms.
forms: intonation: Vous parlez anglais ? ↗
est-ce que + S + V: Est-ce que vous parlez anglais ? (est-ce qu' before a vowel)
inversion: Parlez-vous anglais ? / Pourriez-vous m'aider ?
answers: oui / non / si (contradicting a negative question)

examples.fr: Est-ce que tu as un stylo ? – Oui, tiens.
examples.en: Do you have a pen? – Yes, here.

examples.fr: Pourriez-vous parler plus lentement, s'il vous plaît ?
examples.en: Could you speak more slowly, please?

mastery: Recognises all three forms as the same question
Transforms statements into est-ce que questions, including est-ce qu' before il/elle
Asks five yes/no questions in an interview and answers oui / non / si correctly
commonErrors: (EN) Using do-support (*Fais-tu parler… / *Est-ce que tu fais aimer…)
(EN) *Est-ce que il … (no elision)
(EN) Answering oui to a negative question to contradict it (should be si)
boundaries: Questions with question words are kt:fr-g-question-words; intonation is practised in kt:fr-phon-prosody.
Full inversion with a noun subject (Marie vient-elle ?) is beyond A2.

primitives.binding: Drag word blocks into intonation, est-ce que and inversion frames; the system names the slot rule broken
Same question in three registers (friend, shop, formal letter); learner chooses the form and sees the register change

kcs.label: Grammatical gender of nouns
kcs.term: Le masculin et le féminin des noms
kcs.description: Every French noun is masculine or feminine, and the gender shows on articles, adjectives and pronouns. Gender is learned with each noun (with its article); a few endings are useful clues (-tion, -té, -ette usually feminine; -ment, -age, -eau usually masculine). Nouns for people often have a masculine and a feminine form.
forms: un livre (m.) / une table (f.)
clue endings: la nation, la liberté (f.); le moment, le fromage, le bureau (m.)
people: un ami / une amie, un acteur / une actrice, un boulanger / une boulangère
same form: un/une élève, un/une journaliste
learn nouns with the article: la voiture, le vélo

examples.fr: Une voiture est rouge, un vélo est bleu.
examples.en: One car is red, one bike is blue.

examples.fr: Mon voisin est boulanger, ma voisine est boulangère.
examples.en: My (male) neighbour is a baker; my (female) neighbour is a baker.

mastery: Sorts familiar nouns into masculine and feminine
Gives the feminine form of common person nouns
Uses the right article with 30 high-frequency nouns in speech
commonErrors: (EN) Learning nouns without articles, then guessing gender
(EN) Assuming natural gender for things
(ZH) Not marking gender at all because Chinese has none
boundaries: Articles are kt:fr-g-articles; adjective agreement is kt:fr-g-adjective-agreement.
Gender rules have many exceptions (le musée, la plage); clues are hints, not rules.

primitives.binding: Sort nouns into le/la boxes, first inducing the ending clues, then handling exceptions (le musée, la plage)
Picture → say the noun with its article before reveal; gender errors tracked separately

kcs.label: Plural of nouns
kcs.description: Most nouns add -s in the plural, which is silent; the plural is usually heard only on the article (le/les, un/des) or through liaison. Nouns ending in -eau and -eu add -x; most -al become -aux; -s, -x, -z do not change.
forms: un livre → des livres (s silent)
le gâteau → les gâteaux, le jeu → les jeux
un journal → des journaux, un animal → des animaux
le prix → les prix, le bus → les bus
irregular: un œil → des yeux; monsieur → messieurs, madame → mesdames

examples.fr: Les enfants mangent des gâteaux.
examples.en: The children are eating cakes.

examples.fr: J'ai deux animaux : un chien et un chat.
examples.en: I have two animals: a dog and a cat.

mastery: Says whether a heard phrase is singular or plural using the article and liaison
Writes the plural of regular and -eau/-al nouns
Writes dictated plural noun phrases with the silent -s
commonErrors: (EN) Pronouncing the plural -s
(EN) Omitting -s in writing because it is silent
(EN) *des animals, *des gâteaus
boundaries: Article forms are kt:fr-g-articles.

primitives.binding: Induce -s / -x / -aux from examples, then apply to unseen nouns; each step shows which rule applied
Heard phrases: decide one or several only from the article/liaison

kcs.label: Definite and indefinite articles
kcs.description: French nouns almost always have a determiner. Indefinite un/une/des introduce something new; definite le/la/l'/les refer to something known or to a category in general (J'aime le chocolat). Des has no English equivalent ('some' or nothing).
forms: indefinite: un (m.), une (f.), des (pl.)
definite: le (m.), la (f.), l' (before vowel/mute h), les (pl.)
general sense with definite: J'aime les chats. Le sport, c'est bien.
contractions with à/de: au, aux, du, des (see place prepositions)
after negation un/une/des → de: kt:fr-g-pas-de

examples.fr: J'ai un chat. Le chat s'appelle Moka.
examples.en: I have a cat. The cat is called Moka.

examples.fr: Les Français aiment le pain.
examples.en: French people like bread.

mastery: Chooses un/une/des vs le/la/les in a short text by meaning (new vs known)
Writes l' before vowels and mute h
Uses the definite article for likes and general statements
commonErrors: (EN) Dropping the article as in English generic plurals (*J'aime chats)
(EN) Translating "some" as *quelques for des
(EN) *le hôtel, *la école
(ZH) Omitting articles altogether
boundaries: Partitive articles (du, de la) are kt:fr-g-partitive; de after negation is kt:fr-g-pas-de.

primitives.binding: Same noun in "new" and "known/general" contexts; learner chooses un/le and sees how the meaning changes
Sentence pairs J'aime le café / Je veux un café: learner judges general vs one item

kcs.label: Everyday and personal objects
kcs.description: Names for things people carry and use every day (bag, keys, phone, wallet, glasses, pen, book, computer), used to describe, ask for and locate objects.
forms: un sac, des clés (f.), un portefeuille, un téléphone (portable), des lunettes (f. pl.)
un stylo, un crayon, un cahier, un livre, un ordinateur
une montre, un parapluie, une carte bancaire
une bouteille, un verre, une tasse

examples.fr: Tu as tes clés ? – Oui, elles sont dans mon sac.
examples.en: Have you got your keys? – Yes, they're in my bag.

examples.fr: J'ai perdu mon portefeuille !
examples.en: I've lost my wallet!

mastery: Matches 20 everyday objects to pictures with the right article
Lists the contents of own bag in writing
Describes a lost object to a lost-property clerk
commonErrors: (EN) Using lunettes in the singular
(EN) Missing gender on high-frequency nouns (*un clé)
boundaries: Describing objects is kt:fr-fn-describe-things; colours are kt:fr-lex-clothes.

primitives.binding: Leaving the house: step by step retrieve keys, wallet, phone, umbrella; then re-run with a different destination
Picture of a desk; learner says what is there; checked against the objects in the picture

kcs.label: Il y a: there is, there are
kcs.description: Il y a states existence and is invariable for singular and plural. In the negative it becomes il n'y a pas de. Il y a also means 'ago' with a time expression (kt:fr-g-time-indicators).
forms: Il y a + un/une/des + noun
Il n'y a pas de / d' + noun
Qu'est-ce qu'il y a ? (What is there? / What's wrong?)
Est-ce qu'il y a … ? / Il y a … ?

examples.fr: Dans ma rue, il y a une boulangerie et deux cafés.
examples.en: In my street there is a bakery and two cafés.

examples.fr: Il n'y a pas de métro dans ma ville.
examples.en: There is no underground in my town.

mastery: Distinguishes il y a (existence) from c'est (identification) in gapped sentences
Writes il n'y a pas de correctly
Describes the contents of a room or street in four sentences
commonErrors: (EN) *Il y a sont / *Ils y ont (plural agreement)
(EN) *Il n'y a pas un/des métro
boundaries: Il y a + time ("ago") is kt:fr-g-time-indicators.

primitives.binding: Street picture: learner says il y a / il n'y a pas de for listed items; checked against the picture
Two versions of a room; learners find differences by asking Est-ce qu'il y a … ?

kcs.label: Negation ne … pas and ne … jamais
kcs.term: La négation ne … pas, ne … jamais
kcs.description: Negation surrounds the conjugated verb: ne before it and pas (or jamais 'never') after it. Ne becomes n' before a vowel. In everyday speech ne is often dropped (Je sais pas), but it is kept in writing and careful speech.
forms: ne + verb + pas: Je ne parle pas italien.
n' before a vowel: Il n'aime pas le café.
ne … jamais: Elle ne mange jamais de viande.
with avoir/être: Je ne suis pas français.
spoken: Je sais pas. / C'est pas grave. (ne omitted)

examples.fr: Je n'habite pas à Paris, j'habite à Marseille.
examples.en: I don't live in Paris; I live in Marseille.

examples.fr: Il ne regarde jamais la télé.
examples.en: He never watches TV.

mastery: Identifies whether heard sentences are negative even without ne
Transforms affirmative sentences into ne … pas / ne … jamais
Talks about three things they never do
commonErrors: (EN) *Je ne pas parle (pas before the verb)
(EN) Translating "don't" with *ne fais pas + verb
(EN) *Je ne aime pas (no elision)
boundaries: De after negation is kt:fr-g-pas-de; ne … plus / rien / personne are kt:fr-g-negation-a2; the spoken drop of ne is in kt:fr-soc-spoken-register.

primitives.binding: Place ne and pas/jamais around the verb in new sentences; the system names the slot rule when violated
Spoken sentences with and without ne; learner decides positive or negative

kcs.label: Pas de after negation
kcs.description: After a negation, the indefinite and partitive articles un, une, des, du, de la become de/d' (Je n'ai pas de voiture). The definite article does not change (Je n'aime pas le café). After être the article stays (Ce n'est pas un chat).
forms: J'ai un frère. → Je n'ai pas de frère.
Il y a du pain. → Il n'y a pas de pain.
Elle a des amis. → Elle n'a pas d'amis.
but: Je n'aime pas le fromage. / Ce n'est pas une pomme.

examples.fr: Je n'ai pas de voiture, je prends le bus.
examples.en: I don't have a car; I take the bus.

examples.fr: Il n'y a plus de lait ? – Si, il y a du lait.
examples.en: Is there no more milk? – Yes, there is some milk.

mastery: Chooses de or the full article after a negative verb
Transforms sentences with un/du/des into the negative
Answers questions about what they have/don't have with correct pas de
commonErrors: (EN) *Je n'ai pas une voiture / *pas du pain
(EN) Over-applying: *Ce n'est pas de chat
boundaries: Basic negation is kt:fr-g-negation-ne-pas; partitives are kt:fr-g-partitive.

primitives.binding: Judge negative sentences with un/de/le; classify by rule (after avoir/il y a, after aimer, after être); then write one of each
Apply the article-to-de rule to new sentences step by step

kcs.label: Adjective agreement
kcs.description: Adjectives agree in gender and number with the noun. Most add -e for feminine and -s for plural; some change more (-eux → -euse, -if → -ive, -en → -enne, blanc → blanche, beau → belle). Adjectives already ending in -e do not change in the feminine. Agreement is often heard in the feminine (petit/petite) but not in the plural.
forms: petit / petite / petits / petites
jeune / jeune (already -e)
heureux / heureuse, sportif / sportive, italien / italienne, cher / chère
blanc / blanche, long / longue, gentil / gentille
beau / belle, nouveau / nouvelle, vieux / vieille

examples.fr: Ma sœur est grande et sportive.
examples.en: My sister is tall and sporty.

examples.fr: Les chaussures noires sont chères.
examples.en: The black shoes are expensive.

mastery: Hears whether an adjective is masculine or feminine when the difference is audible (petit/petite)
Writes agreeing forms for regular and common irregular adjectives
Describes two people (one man, one woman) and an object with correct agreement
commonErrors: (EN) Not adding -e in writing when it is silent (*une robe noir)
(EN) Pronouncing petit and petite the same
(EN) Treating colour adjectives as invariable
boundaries: Position of adjectives is kt:fr-g-adjective-position; beau/nouveau/vieux before a vowel (bel, nouvel, vieil) are noted but tested at A2.

primitives.binding: Induce -e/-s and -eux/-euse patterns, then apply to unseen adjectives; the system displays the rule used
Hear il est grand / elle est grande about a picture; decide who is meant from the audible ending

kcs.label: Position of adjectives
kcs.description: Most adjectives follow the noun (un livre intéressant, une voiture rouge). A small set of frequent short adjectives usually comes before (beau, joli, bon, mauvais, grand, petit, jeune, vieux, nouveau, gros, premier).
forms: noun + adjective: un pull noir, une ville moderne
BAGS-type adjectives before: un petit chien, une jolie maison, un bon restaurant, un nouveau téléphone
two adjectives: une petite voiture rouge
des → de before a plural adjective in careful French: de jolies fleurs (des jolies in speech)

examples.fr: J'habite dans une petite maison blanche.
examples.en: I live in a small white house.

examples.fr: C'est un bon restaurant italien.
examples.en: It's a good Italian restaurant.

mastery: Chooses the correct position for common adjectives
Orders word blocks into noun phrases with one or two adjectives
Describes own home and town using four adjective + noun phrases
commonErrors: (EN) Putting colour adjectives before the noun (*une rouge voiture)
(EN) *un restaurant bon
boundaries: Meaning changes with position (un grand homme / un homme grand) are beyond A2.
Agreement is kt:fr-g-adjective-agreement.

primitives.binding: Move the adjective before/after the noun and see which positions are standard; restore the right one
Noun-phrase slots (det – pre-adj – noun – post-adj); the system names the violated slot

kcs.label: Possessive determiners
kcs.description: Possessive determiners agree with the thing possessed, not with the owner: mon/ma/mes, ton/ta/tes, son/sa/ses, notre/nos, votre/vos, leur/leurs. Son and sa both mean his, her or its. Ma/ta/sa become mon/ton/son before a vowel (mon amie).
forms: mon père, ma mère, mes parents
ton / ta / tes; son / sa / ses (his or her)
notre / nos, votre / vos, leur / leurs
before a vowel: mon école, son amie (f.)

examples.fr: Paul aime sa sœur et Marie aime son frère.
examples.en: Paul loves his sister and Marie loves her brother.

examples.fr: Vos billets, s'il vous plaît. – Voilà nos billets.
examples.en: Your tickets, please. – Here are our tickets.

mastery: Chooses son/sa/ses according to the possessed noun
Uses mon before feminine nouns starting with a vowel
Describes a family photo with possessives for several owners
commonErrors: (EN) Choosing son/sa by the owner's gender (*Marie aime sa frère)
(EN) *ma amie
(ZH) Translating 的 with de + pronoun (*le livre de moi)
boundaries: Possessive pronouns (le mien) are kt:fr-g-possessive-pronouns.

primitives.binding: Sentences where only son/sa shows which noun is possessed; learner must look at the noun's gender
Family photo with name tags; learner says whose is what; checked against tags

kcs.label: Demonstrative determiners
kcs.description: Ce, cet, cette, ces mean 'this/that/these/those'. Cet is used before a masculine noun starting with a vowel or mute h. -ci and -là can be added to the noun to contrast near and far.
forms: ce livre, cet ami, cet hôtel, cette maison, ces enfants
ce … -ci / ce … -là: ce pull-ci, ce pull-là
time: ce matin, ce soir, cette semaine, cet été

examples.fr: Je voudrais cette robe, s'il vous plaît.
examples.en: I'd like this dress, please.

examples.fr: Cet hôtel est cher, mais ce restaurant est bon marché.
examples.en: This hotel is expensive, but this restaurant is cheap.

mastery: Chooses ce/cet/cette/ces in gapped noun phrases
Points out items in a shop with ce … -ci / ce … -là
Uses ce matin, cette semaine to locate events
commonErrors: (EN) *ce ami / *ce hôtel
(EN) Using cette for masculine nouns ending in -e (*cette livre)
boundaries: Demonstrative pronouns (celui-ci) are kt:fr-g-demonstrative-pronouns; ça is kt:fr-g-ca.

primitives.binding: Heard ce/cet/cette + noun: pick the object in the picture by gender
Choosing clothes in a shop: learner points with ce/cette … -ci/-là; the assistant branches
